summary: This informational memo declares RFC 4148 and the IANA IPPM Metrics Registry obsolete. The registry was not detailed enough to uniquely identify IP performance metrics, and no one was found who used it. The registry is withdrawn.

eli5.summary: A list that was meant to name network measurements turned out too vague and unused. This note officially throws it away.

subtitle: Why the IP Performance Metrics registry was withdrawn from use.

tldr.problem: The IANA IP Performance Metrics (IPPM) Registry was designed to catalog network measurement metrics, but it turned out to be too vague to uniquely identify metrics, and nobody used it.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC formally reclassifies RFC 4148 as Obsolete and tells IANA to withdraw the registry from further updates. The registry contents remain available for reference, but no new entries can be added.
tldr.outcome: The IPPM Metrics Registry is officially deprecated. Future work on metrics will need a new registry with better structure.

facts.label: Registry name
facts.value: IANA IP Performance Metrics (IPPM) Metrics Registry

today: RFC 6248 is Informational and was published in April 2011. The IANA IP Performance Metrics Registry is marked as Obsolete and no longer accepts new registrations.

sections.title: The Problem with the Registry
sections.content:
The IPPM framework (RFC 2330) describes how to measure network performance in general terms. It uses the concept of "Type P" to represent parameters like packet payload length and protocol type, so metrics can be specified broadly but with the ability to fill in specifics.

When the IPPM Metrics Registry (RFC 4148) was designed, the variability in Type P and the many metric parameters were not fully appreciated. Early metrics only documented Poisson streams, but later work standardized Periodic Stream measurements, adding more variability. It became infeasible to register every possible combination of these parameters in a simple registry structure.
sections.eli5: Network metrics have many parameters that can change: what kind of traffic, how often it's sent, what size packets. The registry couldn't handle all the combinations.

sections.title: Evidence of Non-use
sections.content:
The IPPM Metrics Registry is believed to have very few users, if any. Strong evidence came when RFC 5644 added entries to the registry using incorrect syntax: ":=" instead of "::=" in the formal notation. This error went unnoticed for eight months before someone's parser found it. If anyone had been actively using the registry, this syntax error would have been caught much sooner.

Even the original registry author agreed that the current structure was not efficient and submitted a proposal to create a new registry with better design. Despite efforts to solicit feedback about continued interest in RFC 4148 during the second half of 2010, no one responded.
sections.eli5: A syntax error sat in the registry for months before anyone noticed. If anyone was using it, they would have found the mistake.

sections.title: Declaring Obsolescence
sections.content:
RFC 6248 formally takes two actions:

First, it reclassifies RFC 4148 as Obsolete. Second, it tells IANA to withdraw the IPPM Metrics Registry from further updates and mark it as Obsolete. When a registry is marked Obsolete, IANA stops accepting new registrations, preventing the addition of new metrics.

This does not erase the registry's contents. Existing entries remain available for reference, and if a user were found in the future, they could continue using the current registry. However, new work on metrics will need to establish a replacement registry with a better structure.
sections.eli5: The official action is simple: stop accepting new entries to the registry, and mark the whole registry as obsolete. But the old data stays there for reference.

sections.title: Implications and Next Steps
sections.content:
This RFC also updates four previous RFCs (4737, 5560, 5644, and 6049) that had registered metrics in the now-obsolete registry. By updating these RFCs, the Obsolete status of the registry becomes evident in any documentation that references these metrics.

The memo assumes that parties wishing to establish a replacement registry function will work to specify one with better structure. The lesson is that registries need to account for parameter variability from the start, and that registry adoption should be monitored to ensure registries are actually being used.
sections.eli5: The documents that used the registry are updated to note it's obsolete. Future work will need a better registry with more flexible structure.
